title: Hakeem Olajuwon
wiki_lead:
Hakeem Abdul Olajuwon (born January 21, 1963), nicknamed "the Dream", is a Nigerian and American former professional basketball player who played 18 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA), primarily with the Houston Rockets. He is a two-time NBA champion, two-time NBA Finals MVP, two-time NBA Defensive Player of the Year, and the 1994 NBA MVP. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest players and centers of all time.
Born in Lagos, Nigeria, Olajuwon traveled from his home country to play for the University of Houston under head coach Guy Lewis. His college career for the Cougars included three trips to the Final Four. Olajuwon was drafted by the Houston Rockets with the first overall selection of the 1984 NBA draft, a draft well known for its immense talent, which also included players such as Michael Jordan, Charles Barkley, and John Stockton. He combined with the 7-foot-4-inch (224 cm) Ralph Sampson to form a duo dubbed the "Twin Towers". The two led the Rockets to the 1986 NBA Finals, where they lost in six games to the Boston Celtics. After Sampson was traded to the Golden State Warriors in 1988, Olajuwon became the Rockets' undisputed leader. He led the league in rebounding twice (1989, 1990) and blocks three times (1990, 1991, 1993).
Despite very nearly being traded during a bitter contract dispute before the 1992–93 season, he remained in Houston. He became the first non-American to be an NBA All-Star and start in an NBA All-Star Game, the first non-American to win the NBA MVP, the first non-American to win NBA Defensive Player of the Year, and in the 1993–94 season, he became and remains the only player in NBA history to win the NBA MVP, Defensive Player of the Year, and Finals MVP awards in the same season. His Rockets won back-to-back championships. The Rockets' 1994 championship against the New York Knicks was the first in franchise history, with Olajuwon avenging his college championship loss to Patrick Ewing. The following year, after a lackluster regular season, Olajuwon's Rockets swept Shaquille O'Neal's Orlando Magic in 4 games in the NBA Finals.
Olajuwon was a member of the 1996 Olympic gold medal-winning United States national basketball team, and was selected as one of the 50 Greatest Players in NBA History. He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2008 and the FIBA Hall of Fame in 2016. In October 2021, Olajuwon was honored as one of the league's greatest players of all time by being named to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team. He ended his career as the league's all-time leader in blocks (3,830), is one of four NBA players to record a quadruple-double, and is the all-time leader in 5x5 games (when a player has at least 5 points, 5 rebounds, 5 assists, 5 steals and 5 blocks) with six.

grok_lead: Hakeem Abdul Olajuwon, known as "The Dream," is a Nigerian-American former professional basketball player widely regarded as one of the greatest centers in NBA history. Born on January 21, 1963, in Lagos, Nigeria, he rose from humble beginnings playing soccer and handball to becoming a dominant force in basketball after discovering the sport at age 15. Drafted first overall by the Houston Rockets in 1984, Olajuwon spent 17 seasons with the team, leading them to back-to-back NBA championships in 1994 and 1995, and earning numerous accolades including NBA MVP, two Finals MVPs, and the league's all-time blocks record. After retiring in 2002 following a brief stint with the Toronto Raptors, he transitioned into successful real estate investments, amassing significant wealth while maintaining a low-profile life focused on family and faith. Olajuwon's early career was marked by rapid adaptation and excellence. He moved to the United States in 1980 to attend the University of Houston, where he initially spelled his name "Akeem" before officially changing it to "Hakeem" in 1991. As a Cougar, he led the team to three consecutive NCAA Final Four appearances from 1982 to 1984 and was named the Most Outstanding Player of the 1983 Final Four. His collegiate success, characterized by his unique footwork and defensive prowess, propelled him to the top of the 1984 NBA Draft, where he joined a Rockets franchise in need of a franchise player. In the NBA, Olajuwon's impact was immediate and profound. Over his 18-season career, he amassed 26,946 points, 13,748 rebounds, and a record 3,830 blocks, while earning 12 All-Star selections, six All-NBA First Team honors, and two Defensive Player of the Year awards in 1993 and 1994. His signature "Dream Shake" moveâa series of fakes and pivotsârevolutionized post play, and in the 1995 playoffs, he outdueled legends like David Robinson and Shaquille O'Neal to secure the Rockets' second title. The following year after his first championship, he repeated the feat, becoming the first player since Michael Jordan in 1991 and 1992 to win Finals MVP in consecutive seasons. Inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2008, Olajuwon's legacy extends beyond statistics as a pioneer for international players in the league. Post-retirement, Olajuwon has built a thriving business empire centered on real estate in Houston, Texas, where he flipped properties and developed commercial ventures, contributing to an estimated net worth exceeding $300 million as of 2025. He has also remained active in philanthropy, supporting education and youth programs in Nigeria and the U.S., often through his Muslim faith, while occasionally mentoring current NBA players on footwork and defense. The Houston Rockets retired his jersey number 34 in 2008, cementing his status as a franchise icon.
